While SWAC systems have been deployed and studied worldwide (e.g., Sanjivy et al. 2023), the GeoSWAC concept—defined here as the use of inland wells hydraulically connected to deep, cold seawater cold seawater through permeable geologic formations for building cooling—has not been previously deployed or examined in the peer-reviewed literature. In this study researchers assessed the subsurface, developed a conceptual geothermal model, and evaluated the techno-economic feasibility of applying a GeoSWAC system at the University of Puerto Rico at Río Piedras (UPR-RP), focusing on cooling loads for four representative campus buildings. Modeled hourly loads were developed using EnergyPlus® and benchmarked against existing system capacity, and economic performance was assessed using levelized cost of cooling (LCOC) metrics to compare GeoSWAC with the current chilled water plant. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1.1 Conceptual District Cooling System—GeoSWAC SWAC systems have gained attention as an alternative to electricity-intensive conventional air conditioning in tropical coastal regions (Coony and Johnson 2024). These systems utilize cold seawater, typically drawn from depths of 500 to 1,000 m where temperatures range 4°C–6°C, to supply cooling demand in buildings (Figure 1a) (Hunt et al. 2019, 2022). The cold seawater is pumped using intake pipelines, often extending along the seabed one to several kilometers offshore, and circulated through heat exchangers that transfer the cold energy to a freshwater distribution loop connected to buildings. Because the SWAC system relies primarily on intensive pumping energy and does not require refrigeration cycles, electricity consumption can be reduced by as much as 75%–90% compared to traditional air conditioning (TEC Inc 2009; Lilley et al. 2015). Over the long term, this reduction in electricity consumption leads to substantial operational savings, up to 82% relative to conventional air conditioning (Makai Ocean Engineering 2008). However, the implementation of SWAC systems remains limited due to their high capital costs and the technical and regulatory challenges associated with installing long offshore intake pipelines in coastal environments. To address the limitations associated with conventional SWAC systems, this study proposes a novel adaptation: GeoSWAC. The GeoSWAC concept harnesses the virtually inexhaustible energy of cold, deep ocean water, typically found at depths of around 1,000 m, for building cooling. Rather than relying on long offshore pipelines and intensive pumping energy like traditional SWAC systems, the GeoSWAC concept employs inland wells that are hydrologically connected to deep seawater through permeable geologic formations (Figure 1b). This inland configuration may eliminate the need for extensive marine infrastructure and offers a more feasible solution in regions where offshore construction is technically, environmentally, or economically challenging. Owing to the natural hydraulic pressure gradient, GeoSWAC systems require pumping only to overcome the small hydraulic head difference between seawater and the elevation of the end use.
